narrative:
On the night of 27 April 1945, Lancaster LM719 (H4-M) departed RAF North Luffenham on a 6.5-hour cross-country navigation training exercise with 1653 HCU. Seven men were aboard — six RCAF, one RAF VR. The war in Europe was days from ending.

At 03:14 hrs on 28 April, the aircraft lost control and dived into the grounds of Stoke Rochford Hall. The Board of Enquiry cited icing in cumulonimbus cloud and possible instrument failure; the pitot head had likely iced up. Radio contact had been lost, and rocket flares fired to attract attention went unacknowledged.

Two eyewitnesses, neither interviewed at the time, independently reported fire before impact — one saw an engine ablaze over Colsterworth, the other watched the aircraft descending with fire in the wing toward Stoke Rochford Hall. A lightning strike is a plausible cause of both the fire and the loss of radio communications.

The BOE was critical of the pilot's airmanship, though Flt Lt Guy had only 60 flying hours. Weather was almost certainly the primary factor. All seven crew were killed.
community_connection: In 2002, an anonymous parcel arrived at 8th Canadian Wing HQ, Trenton — an RCAF identity bracelet engraved with Sgt Verle Cline's name and service number, found at the crash site. This led to the identification of the aircraft and all crew. Cline, born in Edmonton but raised in California, had enlisted in the RCAF after the US would not deploy him as a foreign national. His fiancée Marge Hill, who gave him the bracelet in Montreal, learned the full story of his death only in 2002. Separately, a class ring found among Cline's personal effects was traced after eleven months to St Malachy's High School, Saint John, New Brunswick — it belonged to F/O John Travis, the wireless operator. Travis's sister Alleyne Murphy had found her brother's name on the Stoke Rochford memorial page and made contact, learning for the first time how he died. The ring was returned to her at a ceremony at RCAF Trenton on the 65th anniversary of the crash.
memorial_details: Dedicated 19 November 2006 at Stoke Rochford Hall. Over 200 attendees including Canadian relatives, Canadian High Commission, senior RAF officers, and 22 Standards of the RAFA, Royal British Legion, and Ex-Service Associations. Plaque cast from salvaged aircraft metal by Cpl Ian Harrison RAF, RAF Cottesmore. Canadian Maple tree (Acer Rubrum) donated by Stoke Rochford Management Ltd. Registered on the UK Inventory of War Memorials (Imperial War Museum). In October 2010, Alleyne Murphy (Travis's sister) visited from Nova Scotia and funded a dwarf quince shrub beneath the plaque, chosen to flower in late April to coincide with the crash anniversary.
